charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

generationMix.title: Generation by fuel
generationMix.content:
Electricity generated (GWh) broken out by the primary fuel burned -- coal, natural gas, nuclear and solar -- disclosed each period in the 10-K/10-Q generation tables.

For Vistra: this is the fuel-mix transition in one chart. The Comanche Peak and Perry/Beaver Valley acquisitions (Vistra Vision, closed 2024) roughly tripled nuclear output, while coal is a shrinking, retiring share of the fleet and gas remains the largest single block -- the dispatchable capacity that captures price spikes in ERCOT and PJM.

What to watch:

  • Coal's absolute GWh declining as plants retire (not just its share)
  • Nuclear's near-flat output -- it runs at a high, steady capacity factor regardless of price, so its EBITDA contribution is the stable base the Texas/East segments build on
  • Gas generation tracking power-price volatility and summer/winter peak demand (AI data-center load growth shows up here before it shows up in revenue)

capacityMix.title: Generation capacity by fuel
capacityMix.content:
Nameplate generation capacity (MW) by fuel type at period end -- the installed base that generationMix draws on.

For Vistra: total capacity jumped from ~36.7GW (FY2023) to ~43.6GW (FY2025) almost entirely from the Vistra Vision nuclear and renewables/battery acquisitions, not new coal or gas builds -- coal MW has been flat to slightly up only because of life-extension work, not new capacity.

What to watch:

  • Capacity additions concentrated in nuclear/renewables versus fossil
  • Capacity factor (GWh generated / MW available) falling for a fuel signals de-rating or more frequent outages, not just lower dispatch
  • Coal capacity retirements announced but not yet reflected in this series

segmentEbitda.title: Segment Adjusted EBITDA
segmentEbitda.content:
Non-GAAP Adjusted EBITDA by operating segment -- Texas (ERCOT generation), East (PJM/MISO generation, includes the acquired nuclear fleet), West (CAISO/WECC generation) and Retail (TXU Energy and the Northeast/Midwest retail electricity brands) -- as reported in segment disclosures, before corporate/other eliminations.

For Vistra: Texas and East are the volatile, power-price-driven segments (Texas Adjusted EBITDA fell FY2024-to-FY2025 on milder weather and lower spreads even as East rose on the nuclear acquisition); Retail is the natural hedge -- it earns more when wholesale prices are low and retail margins hold up -- which is why the group's blended EBITDA is steadier than any one segment.

What to watch:

  • Texas EBITDA swings with ERCOT summer peak pricing and weather
  • Retail EBITDA moving opposite to Texas/East in a given period (the hedge working)
  • East's step-up from the nuclear acquisition versus organic growth

retailVolume.title: Retail electricity sales volume
retailVolume.content:
Electricity sold to retail (residential/commercial/industrial) customers, in GWh, split between ERCOT (Texas, via TXU Energy) and the Northeast/Midwest retail brands acquired with Vistra Vision.

For Vistra: Retail is the demand-side counterpart to the generation segments -- volume growth here with flattish or falling generation volume means more of the fleet's output is being captively sold rather than merchant-sold into the wholesale market, which is the lower-volatility outcome management targets.

What to watch:

  • ERCOT volume trend versus Texas population/data-center load growth
  • Northeast/Midwest volume, now a full year of Vistra Vision retail customers, versus the legacy ERCOT-only book
  • Volume growth without margin growth (customer additions at thin spreads)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Vistra Corp.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Vistra Corp.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Vistra Corp.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Vistra Corp.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Vistra Corp.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Vistra Corp.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Vistra Corp.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Vistra Corp.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Vistra Corp.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Vistra Corp.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
